opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a very real question, and honestly I don't think there's a single answer. But let me share how I think about it.

First, you have to be honest about one thing: if your product's value is mostly "the model can't do X yet, so we built scaffolding to make it do X," that's a very fragile position. Model capability is improving very fast, and a lot of that scaffolding just gets absorbed into the next model. So many startups that were built around prompt engineering or clever workflows a year or two ago find the base model now does it out of the box. That's the risk everyone already knows.

So where can you actually survive? I think there are a few places.

One is **context**. The model companies are building general intelligence, but intelligence alone doesn't solve a real-world problem. You need the right context: the user's data, the company's internal processes, the domain-specific knowledge, the tools and systems the work actually lives in. If you're deeply embedded in a particular workflow, say legal, healthcare, finance, or some vertical industry, and you own the integration, the data flow, and the trust of that customer, that's something a general model company is not going to prioritize. They're not going to send people to sit with a hospital and understand how their billing system works.

The second is **the environment and the feedback loop**. I think about this a lot from the research side. The models get better through interaction, through reward, through seeing what success looks like on a task. If your product sits where real tasks happen and you can collect signal about what "good" means in that domain, you're building something like a private environment. That's very valuable, and over time it lets you do things the general model can't, or at least can't yet.

The third is **product and user experience**. People underestimate this. The model is like an engine, but people buy cars. How you design the interaction, how the agent communicates with humans, when it asks for help, how it handles mistakes, how it fits into someone's day: these are real problems, and they're not purely solved by a stronger model. Look at how many great products in the internet era were built on top of shared infrastructure. Infrastructure being commoditized doesn't mean the application layer has no value.

But I'd add a caveat. You should build assuming the model will get much better, not hoping it won't. The best wrappers, if you still want to call them that, are the ones whose product gets *better* when the model gets better, not the ones that get replaced. If a new model release makes you nervous, that's a signal. If it makes you excited because your product suddenly works better, you're probably in a good position.

And frankly, speed matters too. Model companies can't do everything. They have to choose. There's a window in many domains, and if you move fast, build real relationships with users, and accumulate data and workflow depth, the window can become a moat.

So my summary would be: don't compete on intelligence, because you'll lose. Compete on context, environment, and product, and make sure you're riding the wave of model progress rather than standing in front of it.

r001.rationale: The response recommends moving fast and building user relationships, data, and workflow depth, but it does not clearly propose capturing substantial user mindshare before model companies react.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose developing the startup’s own model while model companies catch up.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that "wrapper" is a bit of a loaded word, and I actually don't love it. If you look at the history of computing, almost every great application company was a "wrapper" on top of some infrastructure layer. Google was a wrapper on top of the internet. Instagram was a wrapper on top of the phone camera. The question was never whether you sit on top of someone else's platform, it's whether you're creating value that the platform itself can't easily capture.

So when people ask how a startup can survive against OpenAI or Anthropic, I'd reframe the question a bit. The model companies are optimizing for generality. They want one model that does everything reasonably well, and their product surface is necessarily broad. That's actually a weakness in a lot of specific contexts, because being general means you don't deeply understand any single workflow.

What I keep coming back to, from my own research on agents, is that the model is only one piece. When we built things like ReAct or SWE-bench, the lesson wasn't that the model is everything. The lesson was that the environment, the tools, the feedback loops, and the data you collect from real use matter enormously. A model company can train a better base model, but they usually don't own the environment where the work actually happens. If you're building for lawyers or for hardware engineers or for a specific vertical, you can design the scaffolding, the interfaces, the evaluation, and you accumulate a kind of proprietary signal about what "good" looks like in that domain. That's very hard to replicate from the outside.

The second thing is that your product should get better as models get better, not worse. A lot of startups made the mistake of building around a model weakness, like patching hallucinations with some clever retrieval trick. The moment the next model fixes that, your moat is gone. The companies that survive are the ones where a stronger model is a tailwind. You want to be the thing that becomes more valuable when intelligence becomes cheaper.

And honestly, the third thing is just that distribution and trust are real. The model companies can't go talk to every hospital or every factory. There's a huge amount of integration work, of building relationships, of understanding regulation and edge cases, that isn't glamorous and isn't about the model at all. That's where a lot of the actual durable business is.

So I don't think the question is wrapper versus not wrapper. It's whether you've found a place where the general model is a commodity input and the real value is in what you built around it.

r001.rationale: It cites distribution, trust, and domain relationships as durable advantages, but does not propose capturing substantial user mindshare before model companies react.

r002.rationale: It treats models as an input and says startups should benefit from stronger models; it does not propose developing their own model while model companies catch up.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: as the models get better, does your product become more valuable, or does the reason for your product disappear? If you’re mostly compensating for something the model cannot do today, that’s a difficult position. The next model release could solve that problem directly.

But a model is not the same thing as a product. In a particular workflow, you still need to understand what users want, connect to their systems, evaluate whether the result is correct, and handle failures. Those things can be quite difficult, and a model company won’t necessarily do them well for every industry.

So I wouldn’t focus too much on whether something is a “wrapper.” I would ask: what are you accumulating as people use your product? Are you learning something about the task that others don’t know? Are you building a way to measure success and improve? Are you becoming part of a workflow that users depend on? If you have those things, better models can help you deliver more value.

Of course, there’s still competition risk. If your entire product is a general capability that naturally belongs in the model’s interface, you should take that seriously. But there’s a lot of room between having an intelligent model and actually solving someone’s problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses becoming part of a dependable workflow and learning from usage, but does not propose capturing substantial user mindshare before model companies react.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose developing the startup’s own model while model companies catch up.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: as the models get better, does your product become more valuable, or does the reason for your product disappear?

If you’re just taking a model API and adding a nicer interface, that’s a difficult position. The model company can add that interface, and a stronger model might eliminate some of the engineering you’ve done. But calling everything a “wrapper” also misses something. Most software builds on infrastructure somebody else provides. The question is where you create value.

For an AI startup, that could be understanding a particular workflow deeply, integrating with the systems customers already use, and making the whole thing reliable enough that people actually depend on it. A model being able to do a task in a demo is different from a product doing it consistently in a real business.

So I would look for a problem where better models help you deliver more value, while your relationship with the customer and your understanding of the workflow keep improving. You also have to keep moving. You can’t assume that a limitation of today’s models will remain a business opportunity forever.

r001.rationale: The response recommends workflow expertise, customer integration, reliability, and customer relationships, but does not propose capturing substantial user mindshare before model companies react.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose developing the startup’s own model while model companies catch up.
